BREAKING: US annual interest expense is up to a record 18.5% of federal government revenue.

This is officially above the previous record of 18.4% set in 1991.

This percentage has more than QUADRUPLED over the last 4 years as interest expenditures on public debt skyrocketed.

US annual interest expense now stands at a record $1.25 trillion, more than 4x the level seen in 1991.

Meanwhile, the 30Y Treasury yield is trading at ~5.21%, just 13 basis points from its highest level since 2007.

By comparison, the 30-year yield was oscillating at ~8.00% in 1991, underscoring how much the US debt burden has grown since then.

The US debt crisis is in uncharted territory.

🇯🇵 Takaichi has just requested nearly ¥9 trillion for defense spending in 2027. Another sign that Tokyo is entering a new fiscal regime at exactly the wrong time as its debt is finally becoming expensive to carry.

📊 The headline amount is probably only a starting point as around 160 items remain uncosted ahead of the defense plan review due by year-end. Japan wants to accelerate spending on long-range missiles, drones, AI, maritime surveillance and stand-off strike capabilities. As nominal GDP has risen significantly, simply maintaining defense spending at 2% of GDP now means roughly ¥13.8tn a year, versus around ¥11tn previously. If Japan were ever to move closer to the 3.5% level Washington is pushing allies toward, we would be talking about roughly ¥24tn a year.

📈 Obviously, the problem is that Japan is no longer financing all of this in a zero-rate world. Debt-service costs for 2027 are expected to rise toward ¥36.6tn while interest expenses are climbing rapidly. Moreover, every bond that matures is gradually being refinanced at much higher rates. Japan’s average debt maturity, at roughly 9 to 10 years, still protects it from a sudden shock but it also means the increase in interest costs will slowly feed through for years. Meanwhile, Takaichi is stacking up spending commitments in defense, industrial policy, growth support, strategic investment, a temporary consumption-tax cut on food, all without fully closing the fiscal equation.

🤷‍♂️ Then, the BOJ’s dilemma gets even more important. If it tightens enough to support the yen and contain inflation, it puts more pressure on JGBs and debt-service costs. On the other hand, if it protects the bond market too aggressively, it risks renewed yen weakness. It is clear that the tension between monetary policy and fiscal policy is becoming much harder to ignore.

Japan is changing regime before the bond market begins imposing its own limits.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/8JgRWwE6Z4

The market just priced a 60% chance the Fed hikes in September, the biggest tightening bet in months. The bond desks do not believe it.

Warsh has jolted the yield curve three times in four months with speeches and press conferences, then failed to follow through. Long-dated Treasury yields now sit at their highest in about two decades because the bond market has stopped trusting the Fed to control inflation.

This is what years of easy money bought: prices stuck above target, a Fed whose word the market discounts, and a Treasury that just said it will at least double its purchases of 10- to 30-year debt to prop up the market it keeps flooding with supply. The credibility gap is already priced into long yields, and it keeps punishing anyone long duration until Warsh acts instead of talks. $TLT

Warsh has jolted the yield curve three times in four months with speeches and press conferences, then failed to follow through. Long-dated Treasury yields now sit at their highest in about two decades because the bond market has stopped trusting the Fed to control inflation.

This is what years of easy money bought: prices stuck above target, a Fed whose word the market discounts, and a Treasury that just said it will at least double its purchases of 10- to 30-year debt to prop up the market it keeps flooding with supply. The credibility gap is already priced into long yields, and it keeps punishing anyone long duration until Warsh acts instead of talks. $TLT

tweets.text:
A stock trading under the ticker MANE is up nearly 500%, and the company has no approved drug.

Wall Street has decided baldness is the next GLP-1 goldmine. Veradermics ran ~500% since its February IPO and Absci more than doubled, betting on 80 million Americans with hair loss and no new treatment since the 1990s.

These are pre-revenue clinical names in a cash-pay market with no insurance, and the thesis rides on FDA data a year out. One failed trial turns a 500% winner into a 90% loser. Size them like lottery tickets, not like Lilly. $MANE

The Fed's own inflation gauge has run above target for 5.5 years, and the new Fed chair just admitted rates are not even restrictive.

PCE sits at 3.7% against a 2% target. The market is now pricing a 62% chance Warsh raises in September rather than cuts, with more tightening priced by March. The bond market flattened the day he finally sounded willing to do it.

This is the bill for years of money printing arriving late. Flood the system long enough and prices stay hot until someone is forced to tighten into it. Anyone positioned for rate cuts is on the wrong side, and the repricing lands on long duration and every rate-sensitive trade built on easy money.

The best we can say in studying past military conflicts: with the passage of time, the stock market has tended to rise - and the more time that has passed, the more it has risen.

Why?

2 reasons: 1) all wars eventually come to an end, and 2) the economy & earnings, even if impaired in the short run, still tended to grow in the long run despite these conflicts.
